questions.explanation: Most candidates got this one. The minority who missed it chose B, which lists charge as a vector. Charge has magnitude and sign, but no direction, so it is a scalar. Acceleration is the only vector in the row. When the options are a table, check every column before you commit: one wrong cell kills the whole row.

The trap is A. J/s is a correct unit for the watt, but the question asked for SI base units, and the joule is not one of them. Strip it back: W = J/s = N m/s = (kg m/s2) × m/s = kg m2/s3, which is B. Read the words 'base units' as an instruction to reduce everything to kg, m, s and A.

Two 6.0 N forces with 60° between their lines of action give a resultant of 2 × 6.0 × cos 30° = 10.4 N, so C. Weaker candidates chose A as often as the key. That comes from treating the diagram as an equilibrium problem and finding the third force that would close the triangle. Nothing here is in equilibrium. You were asked for the resultant of the two forces, not the force that balances them.

Fewer than half of candidates found the key. Horizontal and vertical motion do not affect each other, but they do share the same time of flight, and that is what links them. The drop obeys y = ½gt<sup>2</sup>, so falling 4y takes twice as long, and at the same horizontal speed twice the time covers twice the distance: 2x. Option A assumes the horizontal distance is unaffected by the height. Option C scales it by 4, the same factor as the drop.

At P the sphere is still speeding up, just less sharply than before, because the graph is still rising. Still accelerating downwards means the weight is still larger than the air resistance, which is C. Option D shows air resistance larger than weight, and that would mean the sphere is slowing down. It was the most popular wrong answer, and it comes from reading a decreasing acceleration as a negative one. They are not the same thing.

Momentum is conserved when no resultant external force acts on the system. That is what 'isolated system' means, and it is the part of the principle candidates most often leave out. A significant minority still chose A, 'in all collisions', even with the correct condition sitting in front of them as option C. The syllabus asks you to state the principle of conservation of momentum, so learn the condition as part of the statement rather than as an afterthought.

The gradient of a momentum-time graph is the resultant force: 5000 / 10 = 500 N. This is Newton's second law in the form F = Δp / Δt. A large majority handled it. Bank the habit for harder graph questions: before calculating anything, ask what the gradient represents and what the area represents.

Candidates split almost evenly between A, B and C, so this was one of the hardest questions on the paper. Start with Newton's second law including both forces: F − W = ma. The rocket's mass is W/g, so F = Wa/g + W. The engine has to supply the resultant force and hold up the weight. Option B is the resultant force alone; option C subtracts the weight instead of adding it. Draw both arrows before you write the equation.

Take moments about the hinge at X. F acts perpendicular to the rod at the far end, at distance L. The weight acts at the midpoint, at distance L/2, and only its component perpendicular to the rod has a turning effect: 28 cos 40°. So F × L = 28 cos 40° × L/2, giving F = 10.7 N, which rounds to 11 N. Weaker candidates went overwhelmingly for C (28 sin 40° = 18 N) and D (28 cos 40° = 21 N). Both are just components of the weight, resolved correctly and then used without accounting for the different distances of F and the weight from the pivot.

Well answered, and it shows good handling of energy conservation. All three stores are non-zero only while he is still falling with the cord already stretching: he still has height above the ground (gravitational), he is still moving (kinetic), and the cord is extended (elastic). At the bottom he is stationary, so kinetic is zero. Before the cord starts to extend, elastic is zero.

'Work done per unit time' is power. You already have v, so P = Fv leaves exactly one missing quantity: the force. That is A. Many candidates chose B, the distance travelled per unit time, which is the velocity the question had already given them. Translate the phrase into the physical quantity first, then look at the options and see what you are still short of.

A very challenging question, and all four options were chosen frequently. Start with the wave type: sound is longitudinal, so the particles oscillate along the direction of travel, left and right. That rules out C and D straight away. The graph shows displacement against distance at one instant, with displacement to the right counted as positive, and the wave travels to the right. Each particle next takes the displacement currently held by the particle on its left. At Y that displacement is more negative, so the particle is moving to the left, back towards the source: B.

Malus's law, applied twice. At the first filter the incoming light is vertically polarised and the axis is 50° from vertical: I = 8.0 cos<sup>2</sup>50° = 3.3 W/m<sup>2</sup>. At the second filter the angle you need is the one between the two transmission axes, 30°, not the 20° to the vertical. 3.3 cos<sup>2</sup>30° = 2.5 W/m<sup>2</sup>, which is B. Using 20° gives 2.9 W/m<sup>2</sup>, option C, and that was the commonest wrong answer. The 30° is stated in the question text.

Five bright fringes span 34 mm, but five fringes have four gaps between them, so the fringe spacing is 34 / 4 = 8.5 mm. Then a = λD / x = (680 × 10<sup>-9</sup> × 2.4) / (8.5 × 10<sup>-3</sup>) = 1.9 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m, option C. Dividing by 5 instead of 4 gives 2.4 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m, which is option B and was the commonest error. Count the gaps, not the fringes.

Candidates struggled here, and the responses were spread across all four options. P and Q lie in the same loop, between the same pair of nodes. Every particle within one loop of a stationary wave vibrates in phase: they reach maximum displacement together and pass through zero together. That is D. They do not have equal amplitude, because P is nearer the antinode than Q, so B is wrong. Frequency and period are the same for every particle on the spring, which rules out A and C.

P is the filament lamp: the curve bends over because the filament heats up, its resistance rises, and each extra volt buys less extra current. R is the diode: almost no current until the forward threshold, then a steep rise. That is row A. Weaker candidates could usually identify one of the two graphs and then guessed the other, which is why B and C were about as popular as the key among them. Both characteristics are named learning outcomes in the syllabus, so learn them as a pair.

Even among the strongest candidates only about half found the key, so take it in steps rather than trying to see the whole circuit at once. The p.d. across the 2.0 Ω resistor is 3.0 × 2.0 = 6.0 V. Now go round the left-hand loop: 9.0 − 6.0 − 1.0 = 2.0 V across P. Kirchhoff's first law at the junction gives the current in the middle branch: 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 A. So R = V / I = 2.0 / 5.0 = 0.40 Ω, option A. Two laws, four lines of working.

Well answered. At the first junction I1 splits into I2 and I3, and I3 then splits into I4 and I5. So I1 = I2 + I3 = I2 + I4 + I5, and options B and D are those same two statements rearranged. Option C claims I2 = I3 + I4 + I5, which counts I3 twice. The question asked which equation is not correct, so C is the answer.

Easy for most candidates. Plutonium-239 has proton number 94 and nucleon number 239, so it has 239 − 94 = 145 neutrons. Those two columns eliminate C and D, and very few candidates fell for them. The charge on W is +1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C, one elementary charge positive, so one electron has been removed from the neutral atom: 93 electrons, option A. The small number who chose B read the charge as negative and added an electron instead of removing one.

The positron is the antiparticle of the electron, and it belongs to the same family: the leptons. The syllabus names electrons and neutrinos as leptons, and defines a hadron as either a baryon (three quarks) or a meson (one quark and one antiquark). So a meson is a hadron, a proton is a hadron, and a quark is not a lepton by definition. The three wrong options were chosen about equally often, which is the signature of guessing. Learn the classes with one example of each.
